title: Zhaozhou's mu
hook: a monk asks if a dog has Buddha-nature. the teacher answers with one syllable.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: koan, a question that won't let you be clever. Your line was one hand.

A monk bows to the old Chinese teacher Zhaozhou, the same teacher who once sent a newcomer to wash his bowl, back on day forty-seven. This monk has heard the teaching that living beings have Buddha-nature, the capacity to wake up. So he points at the humblest example he can find. Does a dog have Buddha-nature, or not? The expected answer is yes. Zhaozhou says one syllable: mu. In Chinese and Japanese, it means something like no, or not, or there isn't. A question, a single word, and a puzzle that has kept students sitting ever since.
screen: `DOES A DOG HAVE BUDDHA-NATURE?` → `THE EXPECTED ANSWER: YES.` → `ZHAOZHOU: MU.`

segments.voice: In the collection called The Gateless Gate, gathered by the Chinese teacher Wumen, Zhaozhou's mu is the first case. First, the surface. Read flatly, Zhaozhou seems to contradict the teaching the monk was repeating. If everything has Buddha-nature, why say no? That's exactly the hook: the no doesn't fit, so the mind can't file it away. Second, it isn't a vote on dogs. Zen teachers say the point isn't a yes or no about animals. Some records even have Zhaozhou answering the same question differently on another day, with a yes. That alone suggests the word is doing something other than giving information. Third, Wumen's comment. Right after the case, he tells the student how to work on it, in vivid pictures. In paraphrase: put your whole body into this mu, day and night. Don't take it as nothing, and don't take it as the opposite of something. It's like swallowing a red-hot iron ball you can't spit out. Fourth, what's left. Wumen's promise, again paraphrased, is that when the work ripens, inside and outside become one, and the student knows it the way someone who can't speak knows their own dream. So mu ends up less like an answer and more like a door. That's why the book is called The Gateless Gate.
screen: `THE FIRST CASE IN THE GATELESS GATE.` · `THE NO DOESN'T FIT.` · `NOT A VOTE ON DOGS.` · `A RED-HOT IRON BALL.`

segments.voice: Sit upright, eyes soft, and let the breath come in on its own. On each out-breath, silently let the syllable ride all the way out, muuu, without thinking what it means or making it yes or no; when the mind wanders, the next out-breath is another mu. Another day, you might try three minutes.
Zhaozhou's mu. A teacher's one-syllable answer, something like no, to a monk's question about a dog. The first case in The Gateless Gate. Today's word.
Your line: mu. One syllable, breathed until it stops being a word about something and is just there. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Rinzai and some other Zen lineages, students are often given mu as a first koan and work on it during sitting, breathing the syllable and bringing their response to a teacher.
